title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #10 (9 July 2026)
content:
The tenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as of 9 July. It also includes the priorities of IOM’s Funding Appeal to scale up urgent assistance.

Highlights

In La Guaira, IOM and its partners strengthened assistance in transitory camps. At César Nieves Stadium, they continued improving spaces and distributed tarpaulins and kitchen sets, while at José María Vargas Sports Centre, services were expanded to include dental and psychiatric care, reaching 290 health and mental health consultations.

To date, IOM has reached 4,526 unique individuals through 7,273 assistance and distribution services, mainly in health, shelter and site coordination, and protection.

IOM maintains its USD 98 million Funding Appeal to assist 850,000 people and support 140 entities between July and December 2026.

IOM Activities

IOM continues supporting prioritized transitory camps in La Guaira, including César Nieves Stadium, José María Vargas Sports Centre and Playa Grande, through site coordination, shelter, registration, WASH, health and mental health, protection and information management.

At César Nieves Stadium, 341 tarpaulins and 334 kitchen sets were distributed. To date, 830 tarpaulins and 825 kitchen sets have been delivered.

At José María Vargas Sports Centre, a team of 12 professionals provided 290 health and mental health consultations, including dental care, internal medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics, psychiatry and psychology.

Registration continued at César Nieves Stadium, covering 489 families and 1,479 individuals, and at Playa Grande, covering 54 families and 160 individuals. Progress was also made on the Rapid Needs Assessment and on information management support to the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue focusing on the improvement and management of transitory camps, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, needs assessments, mobility monitoring and inter-agency coordination.

Additional funding would enable IOM to scale up shelter assistance, essential items, early recovery, protection, health and mental health, data, DTM and coordination support.

title: Ebola Outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda - External update #3 - 10 July 2026
content:
Highlights

• The seventeenth Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to evolve, with 1,792 confirmed cases, including 625 deaths and 295 recoveries, reported across 37 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu as of 8 July. The Government has also reported two confirmed cases in Kisangani, Tshopo Province.

• The outbreak is unfolding in an area marked by persistent insecurity and displacement due to armed clashes, limiting humanitarian access and complicating Ebola prevention, surveillance and response. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 91 per cent of confirmed cases and nearly 86 per cent of deaths.

• While no Ebola cases have been reported among refugees in the DRC to date, 19 internally displaced persons (IDPs) from the Kpangba, Kigonze and Bembeyi sites in Ituri are among confirmed cases. More than 2 million forcibly displaced people live in Ebola-affected or high-risk areas of eastern DRC, including 320,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, heightening the urgency of inclusive preparedness, risk communication, surveillance and access to national response systems.

• In Uganda, the outbreak remains relatively contained, with 20 confirmed cases as of 9 July, including two deaths, 17 recoveries and one patient currently admitted for care.

• UNHCR is supporting the Governments of the DRC and Uganda, alongside the World Health Organization (WHO), other United Nations agencies and local communities, to strengthen Ebola prevention and response and ensure that refugees, asylum-seekers, IDPs and host communities can access information, surveillance and essential services.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 75, as of 7 July, 2026
crisis: Central African Republic: Cholera Outbreak - Jun 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Critical humanitarian situation in Am-Dafock following recent clashes
  • Heavy rains cause human and property damage in Ngaoundaye
  • Rafaï: More than 300 displaced and other vulnerable families receive livestock and poultry

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • More than 1,000 people have fled from Zemio to Zapaï in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) out of fear for their safety, following the killing on 27 July of a religious leader who had been actively involved in community reconciliation efforts in the area. An unknown number of residents have also undertaken preventive displacement within Zemio town since the end of June, driven by fears of possible clashes between parties to the conflict. Communities are additionally living in fear of reprisals over alleged collaboration with one or another party to the conflict, limiting opportunities for community engagement activities. Furthermore, a local authority was killed by armed men on 5 July along the Dembia axis, while businesses in Zemio town were robbed, further exacerbating the climate of fear affecting the population.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • On 2 July, humanitarian partners conducted a rapid humanitarian assessment in Am-Dafock, along the border with Sudan, with logistical support from MINUSCA, following the clashes that occurred in the town on 30 June. The assessment found that the humanitarian situation remains critical, with the most urgent needs relating to protection, health care and access to safe drinking water. The town’s only health facility had been looted and was occupied by armed elements at the time of the assessment. The only accessible water point is insufficient to meet the needs of the affected population. In addition, displaced people are unable to leave the site because of security concerns. A MINUSCA helicopter rotation on 4 July enabled the delivery of emergency assistance provided by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), International Medical Corps (IMC), the Central African Red Cross and an international orgnaization. The assistance included 425 tarpaulins, 680 buckets, medicines and hospital consumables, personal protective equipment and body bags. IMC is currently operating mobile clinics in Am-Dafock and has already provided essential health services to at least 140 people. However, logistical constraints continue to hamper the scale-up of the humanitarian response, as the main access road has become impassable during the ongoing rainy season. Approximately 24 metric tons of humanitarian cargo remain to be transported, including protection supplies, first-aid kits, soap, gloves and protective masks. With an estimated airlift capacity of two metric tons per helicopter rotation, at least 12 additional rotations will be required to deliver all pending relief items. Consequently, delays in the delivery of humanitarian assistance are expected, which could affect the timely provision of life-saving aid to affected populations.

Food Security

Nana-Gribizi Prefecture – Center

  • From 22 June to 3 July, Welthungerhilfe (WHH) conducted an agricultural entrepreneurship training program for 230 members from 11 agricultural groups, including 142 women and 88 men. Participants strengthened their skills in business management, planning, marketing, and the organization of agricultural activities. In addition, 37 members of two pastoral groups, including 26 women, received training on good livestock management practices, with a focus on animal nutrition, animal health, and reproduction. To further improve agricultural production practices, 166 lead farmers and technical focal points were trained in Kaga-Bandoro, Ouandago, and Mbrès. The training sessions covered good agricultural practices as well as crop-specific technical production packages tailored to several priority crops.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #6 (July 9, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE is steadily expanding its earthquake response across northern Venezuela, shifting more attention to urgent health needs and the prevention of subsequent public health crises. The team has increased the reach of mobile medical teams; reinforced primary health facilities; broadened water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) efforts; and is expanding mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) to assist additional earthquake-affected communities. Preventing disease outbreaks and maintaining consistent access to care remain central priorities as thousands of people navigate uncertainty while living in temporary settlements or damaged neighborhoods.

Situation Overview

Humanitarian needs remain significant as response efforts continue. The death toll has been reported at over 3,800, with over 16,700 injuries, and approximately 17,800 displaced and/or homeless people. While debris removal and structural assessments are progressing, thousands of people remain affected and require humanitarian assistance. Health partners remain concerned about deteriorating sanitation conditions, limited access to clean water, and disruptions to routine healthcare, all of which increase the risk of secondary public health emergencies. Project HOPE’s teams continue to report increased cases of diarrheal disease, skin infections, urinary tract infections, dehydration, and respiratory illnesses, with mental health needs remaining high among families coping with displacement and uncertainty. Rainfall and overcrowded shelters are also creating favorable conditions for the spread of infectious diseases, reinforcing the importance of disease surveillance and WASH interventions.

title: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 8 (29 June - 5 July 2026)
content:
According to the World Health Organization, as of 4 July, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has confirmed more than 1,500 cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD). As of 5 July, Uganda has confirmed 20 cases, with no new cases during the reporting period.

Cross-border movements, displacement and population mobility are shaping disease transmission, requiring an urgent and rapid response to save lives and protect people on the move, while mitigating regional health risks. Given the unfolding public health risks, IOM’s preparedness and response efforts focus on supporting cross-border communities, points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs) to inform and guide broader public health interventions.

In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) system-wide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM is scaling up its response, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries.
IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where active outbreak response operations are ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of cross-border transmission.
Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries,
Angola, the Central African Republic, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level.

title: Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #6 (South-West Efate, Shefa Province)
content:
Key highlights include:

  • Nine new laboratory-confirmed dengue cases were reported during Epidemiological Week (EW) 27, bringing the cumulative total to 38 confirmed cases.
  • Weekly case numbers remain above the outbreak alert threshold of four cases per week, indicating ongoing dengue virus transmission.
  • Six cases (15.8%) have required hospitalization since the outbreak began. Of these, one patient remains hospitalized, while five have recovered and been discharged.
  • No dengue-related deaths have been reported to date.
  • The most affected locations are:
    • Pango Area Council – 34% of cases
    • Eratap Area Council – 21% of cases
  • Additional cases have been reported from Erakor, Eton, Port Vila, and Mele, indicating a widening geographic spread.
  • Males account for 55% of reported cases, and 64% of cases have occurred among individuals under 26 years of age.
  • Epidemiological investigations continue to identify evidence of local transmission.
  • Laboratory testing has confirmed the circulating strain as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1). All five samples tested were identified as DENV-1.
  • There has been no significant change in the outbreak situation since the previous report. Therefore, the outbreak status remains unchanged, and enhanced surveillance and response measures continue.

title: UNHCR Facilitated Return of Syrian Refugees - Lebanon, 30 June 2026
content: Since the escalation of hostilities on 2 March 2026, and until 30 June, the Syrian General Authority for Border and Customs (GABC) estimates that 581,409 Syrians crossed from Lebanon into Syria, while the Lebanese General Security (GSO) estimates that 491,265 Syrians departed through Ocial Crossing Points (OCPs) between 2 March and 26 June. While some movements to Syria were driven by the conflict in Lebanon, others reflect previously planned movements. Syrians crossing include people known, and not known to UNHCR, namely both refugees and Syrians who have stayed in Lebanon under various visa and sponsorship arrangements or returning from temporary visits. During June, a slight increase was observed in daily movement to Syria, with over 4,500 Syrians crossing per day through OCPs, mainly due to the end of the school academic year and the start of the summer season. As of the end of June 2026, only 6% (29,054 individuals) of Syrians who left Lebanon through the OCPs, based on GSO and UNHCR Syria data*, have so far been verified to be known to UNHCR**. Further verification, data collection and triangulation are ongoing.

title: Middle East Situation Lebanon - Flash Update #14 (22 June - 05 July 2026)
content:
• As of 6 July, almost 500,000 individuals remain internally displaced within Lebanon, as many families are unable to return to their home areas due to inaccessibility, destruction or continued insecurity.

• Protection monitoring shows a shift from large-scale displacement towards more complex return and local integration dynamics. While the overall number of displaced people is declining, those who remain displaced are facing growing challenges, including difficulty accessing adequate housing, worsening economic conditions, increased protection risks for women and children, and weakened social cohesion within communities.

• Returns to conflict-affected areas in Lebanon are taking place more quickly among Lebanese internally displaced persons (IDPs) than among displaced refugees. For Syrian refugees, returns to the South remain limited due to a mix of protection, legal, housing, and economic barriers. Rising rental costs, limited availability of affordable housing, unpaid rent debts, and, in some areas, additional municipal requirements continue to make access to housing and durable solutions more difficult.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 302: Week 1 – July 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Exchange Rate and Trade Dynamics:

• Exchange Rate: During the first week of July, the Afghani depreciated to AFN 65.7/USD, weakening by 1.7% compared to the previous week. Despite this decline, the currency remained 5% stronger than last year and 13% stronger than the three-year average, continuing to provide some support in containing imported inflation.

• Trade: Market supply remained generally adequate, supported by domestic harvests and ongoing regional trade. However, Afghanistan's dependence on imported goods continues to expose domestic markets to fluctuations in the exchange rate, fuel costs, and regional trade conditions, which contribute to price volatility across the country and expose the economy to external vulnerabilities.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed divergent trends during the first week of July, with modest weekly changes across most staples.

• Wheat and Flour: Wheat grain prices rose marginally this week, while high-price and low-price flour also recorded moderate increases. On an annual basis, wheat grain (+13%), high-price flour (+7%), and low-price flour (+11%) remained elevated, mainly due to higher transportation costs associated with renewed import routes.

• Rice: Both rice categories declined slightly this week. Despite these weekly decreases, rice prices remained significantly higher than last year (high-quality +27%; low-quality +34%) and above the three-year average level.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil, pulses, sugar and salt prices edged down this week. Sugar posted a notable weekly drop, though it remained above last year's levels (+9%). Cooking oil prices held steady, staying negligibly above last year (+2%). Salt declined weekly but remained higher year-on-year (+8%).

• Vegetables: Seasonal harvests continued to support domestic vegetable markets with slight weekly fluctuations. Compared to the previous week, tomato (+2.3%) and onion (+2.5%) prices rose slightly, while potato prices remained broadly stable (-0.6%). Compared to last year and the three-year average, potato and tomato prices remains significantly higher, while onion prices have declined.

Non-Food Items:

• Fuel: Diesel prices rose by 7.2% during the week, mainly reflecting reduced fuel imports, particularly from Russia. Compared to last year and the three-year average, diesel prices remained 9% and 12% higher, respectively.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices changed only marginally, with DAP declining by 0.2% and Urea by 1.4% over the week. Compared to last year, DAP and Urea prices remained considerably higher (+17% and +49%, respectively), while improved seed and animal feed prices continued to remain below both last year and the three-year average.

• Livestock: The price of a one-year-old live female sheep declined marginally (-0.4%) during the week and was 5% below last year's level and 2% below the three-year average, contributing to slightly weaker pastoralist ToT.

Labour Market:

• Labour market conditions remained subdued. The unskilled labour wage declined marginally (-0.5%), while labour availability remains low at 1.9 days per week. Labour availability remained 18% below both last year's level and the three-year average, underscoring continued pressure on household income opportunities for casual labourers

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Lebanon Crisis (23 June - 7 July 2026)
content:
The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains fragile despite a reduction in hostilities, with significant and persistent humanitarian, protection, and early recovery needs. Daily airstrikes and military operations, particularly in southern Lebanon, continue to pose risks to civilians and limit safe returns, highlighting the potential for renewed escalation despite ongoing diplomatic efforts. Since 2 March 2026, a reported 4,304 people have been killed and 12,203 have been injured.

Women and girls are bearing the brunt of the crisis, facing heightened protection and gender-based violence (GBV) risks, disrupted health services, including for maternal health, and reduced access to safe and dignified support.

Since the onset of the crisis, UNFPA has reached over 150,000 displaced people with sexual and reproductive health and GBV services. These services have been delivered through support to 55 health facilities, nine mobile medical units, 24 mobile GBV teams, and 19 women and girls’ safe spaces, serving collective shelters and host communities.

UNFPA launched a revised Flash Appeal in June, aligned with the revised Inter-Agency Lebanon Flash Appeal appealing for US $25 million to meet the urgent needs of 450,000 people from March to August 2026. To date, only 16 per cent of the required funding has been secured.

title: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #3 (2026-07-09)
content:
Description

Despite the weakening of Typhoon Maysak, its circulation, combined with prevailing weather conditions, has continued to bring heavy rainfall to the northern mountainous provinces of Viet Nam, increasing the risk of flash floods, landslides and localised flooding.

According to the Vietnam Disaster and Dyke Management Authority (VDDMA), heavy rainfall is expected to continue across parts of the northern mountainous region over the coming days. Local authorities have been instructed to maintain 24-hour duty rosters, closely monitor weather developments, and continue preparedness and response activities, while central and Central Highlands provinces strengthen preparedness measures ahead of the peak disaster season.

According to rapid reports from the Departments of Agriculture and Environment of Lai Chau and Dien Bien provinces, heavy rainfall and landslides that occurred between 7 and 8 July 2026 caused significant damage to housing, agriculture, and transportation infrastructure. In Lai Chau Province, three houses were destroyed, 18 houses were damaged by landslides and five additional houses were affected. In Dien Bien Province, six houses were damaged by landslides and three additional houses were affected. Agricultural losses in Lai Chau included damage to 40.5 hectares of rice fields and crops, the loss of 17 livestock and 0.76 hectares of fishponds washed away.

Transportation infrastructure was also significantly affected. Landslides and road damage disrupted traffic along National Highway 279 in Dien Bien Province, National Highway 4D in Lai Chau Province, as well as several provincial, inter-commune and village roads in both provinces. Local authorities immediately mobilised personnel and heavy equipment to clear landslides, restore road access and assist affected households with early recovery activities.

Separately, a whirlwind lasting approximately 15 minutes struck Binh Thanh Commune, Hung Yen Province, on the afternoon of 8 July, damaging tiled and metal roofs of several houses. Affected households have started repairing the damage using their own resources.

Weather forecasts indicate that heavy rainfall may continue across the northern mountainous region, increasing the risk of additional flash floods, landslides and localized flooding. Authorities continue to monitor the situation closely while conducting damage assessments and preparedness activities in areas at risk.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Situation Report-4, Monsoon depression in Cox’s Bazar (2026-07-09)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

The well-marked low persists over Northwest Madhya Pradesh & adjoining area. It is very likely to move north-northwestwards and recurve northeastwards thereafter. Under its influence steep pressure gradient persists over North Bay and adjoining area. The axis of monsoon trough runs through Rajasthan, the center of the wellmarked low, Bihar, West Bengal to Assam across southern part of Bangladesh. Monsoon is active over Bangladesh and strong over North Bay. According to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), active monsoon conditions are expected to continue until at least 11 July, with heavy to very heavy rainfall forecast across Cox's Bazar and the Chattogram Division. The five-day rainfall forecast indicates that very heavy rainfall (≥88 mm/day) is expected across several sub-districts of Cox’s Bazar between 9–12 July, with Ukhiya forecast to receive the highest and most persistent rainfall. Teknaf, Maheshkhali, Kutubdia, Ramu, Cox’s Bazar Sadar, and Chakaria are also expected to experience very heavy rainfall on multiple days. Rainfall is expected to decrease significantly across all sub-districts on 13 July, reducing light to moderate levels. The prolonged period of intense rainfall during 9–12 July may increase the risk of flash flooding, waterlogging, landslides, and localized disruptions, particularly in the highly affected areas. A BMD landslide warning forecasts 200–500 mm of rainfall between 9 and 11 July, maintaining a high landslide risk in Teknaf, Ukhiya, and Cox's Bazar Sadar. The Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG) Anticipatory Impact Analysis continues to identify Cox's Bazar as highly vulnerable to flash flooding. Continued rainfall is expected to increase the risk of flooding, landslides, infrastructure damage, access constraints, and displacement. Humanitarian partners should maintain heightened preparedness, monitor weather advisories and high-risk locations, disseminate early warning messages, support relocations where necessary, and exercise caution during field movements.

Risk Analysis

Across the 33 Camps: Between 5 and 9 July 2026, a total of 304 weather-related incidents were reported, affecting 5,863 households (28,091 people) across the 33 camps. The incident caused damage to 3,127 shelters and displaced 4,732 individuals. To date, *15 fatalities and 18 injuries have been recorded. These figures underscore the significant humanitarian impact of the ongoing monsoon conditions and highlight the need for continued monitoring, preparedness, and response efforts, particularly in areas at heightened risk of flooding, water logging, and landslides. title: Georgia Pluvial/Flash Flood in Eastern Georgia 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRGE020)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

01-10-2025

What happened, where and when?

At the end of September 2025, heavy and prolonged rainfall struck eastern Georgia, with Lagodekhi Municipality in Kakheti, experiencing the most severe impact. Rising river levels and overflows triggered flash floods across at least 13 villages, including Kabali, Ninighori, Giorgeti, Tsodniskari, and nearby communities. Floodwater damaged ground floors of the residential houses, courtyards, and farmland, destroying household belongings, food stocks, and agricultural inputs. Several road sections were submerged, restricting mobility and access to essential services for several days. As the municipal authorities started with infrastructure rebuilding and accounting for overall scope of the disaster, GRCS engaged in the response by mobilizing staff and volunteers from Lagodekhi and neighboring branches to conduct rapid needs assessment and plan for targeted assistance as per official request of the municipal authorities.

title: Ukraine Situation - Moldova : Protection Working Group - UNHCR: Protection Brief #8 July 2026
content:
Operational Context & Analysis

As of 31 May 2026, more than 1.25 million refugees had arrived in the Republic of Moldova1 from Ukraine since 24 February 2022. While most continued westward to the EU, around 140,000 Ukrainian refugees, of whom 64% were female, and 48% were children are in the territory of Moldova. To enhance and promote evidence-based protection interventions throughout the country, UNHCR has been actively engaged in monitoring, documenting, and analysing the profiles, needs, and intentions of refugees through ongoing protection monitoring in accommodation sites, centres for humanitarian aid distribution, Community Service Centres (CSC), and other locations. 2 This report encompasses the findings from 248 interviews conducted with Ukrainian refugee households, comprising 426 household members, conducted between 1 May and 30 April 2026. Reference is also made to the Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) conducted by UNHCR and its partners over the same period. 3 This report also draws from the sector discussions within the Protection Working Group4 , and the Inclusion and Solution Working Group and the labour market analysis on refugee participation conducted in 20265 .

title: UNHCR Afghanistan Protection Monitoring 1st Quarter 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In Afghanistan’s complex protection context, characterized by continued returns, ongoing displacement, economic hardship, and sustained protection risks, Community-Based Protection Monitoring (CBPM) plays a central role in informing protection analysis and response. CBPM enables UNHCR and partners to systematically collect community-reported information on protection risks, vulnerabilities, and coping mechanisms affecting returnees, internally displaced persons, and host communities. By generating regular, area-specific evidence, CBPM supports the identification of priority protection concerns, facilitates the monitoring of protection trends over time, and informs UNHCR programming, coordination, and advocacy efforts. The analysis presented in this report is based on data collected through UNHCR’s CBPM tools in the first quarter of 2026, including household-level surveys, key informant interviews (KIIs), and focus group discussions (FGDs). These tools are designed to generate evidence-based information on the protection needs and risks faced by returnee, displaced, and host communities, and to inform UNHCR programming, strategic decision-making, and advocacy, while also feeding into the Afghanistan Protection Cluster's analysis and information products. Survey locations are selected based on the concentration of returnees and displaced populations. The CBPM covers UNHCR population groups of concern, including returnees, internally displaced persons (IDPs), IDP returnees, refugees and asylum seekers, as well as members of host communities. This report presents the findings and analysis of the CBPM exercise for the first quarter of 2026, providing an overview of key protection trends and highlighting the main findings during the period from January to March 2026.

title: Venezuela Protection Situation Update #3 - Earthquake Response
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On the 24th of June 2026, two earthquakes of 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes affected the centre-north of Venezuela, with particularly severe consequences in the states of La Guaira and Grand Caracas. After 12 days, the emergency continues to evolve in a context marked by internal displacement, temporary shelter arrangements for affected populations in formal or informal collective spaces, persistent disruptions in access to services, and growing demand for humanitarian assistance and protection mechanisms.

The available information shows that protection needs continue to rise among the population affected by the earthquakes. In addition, the effects of the emergency are not strictly limited to the areas directly impacted, as population displacements have been observed toward host communities and other states in the country, including Bolívar, Delta Amacuro, Anzoátegui, Sucre, Zulia, Táchira, and Apure. The loss of homes, displacement, stays in temporary government-managed shelters and informal accommodation sites, as well as the disruption or weakening of family, community, institutional, and protection networks, have increased exposure to protection risks and reduced the coping capacity of affected communities.

Assessments conducted identify significant concerns related to mental health and psychosocial support needs, family separation, inadequate privacy and security in accommodation facilities, and the loss of personal documentation, which may affect access to assistance and essential services. These risks disproportionately affect children and adolescents, women, older persons, persons with disabilities, and other individuals with specific protection needs. In this context, the sector’s priorities continue to focus on strengthening protection mechanisms for the most vulnerable populations, increasing access to specialised services, and helping ensure that affected people can access humanitarian assistance and available services safely and with dignity.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #41 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 6 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,319 deaths and 12,203 injuries due to hostilities recorded by the Ministry of Public Health since 2 March.
  • 646,107 people have returned to their areas of origin, while around 500,000 people remain displaced, including 37,000 Internally Displaced Persons (over 53 per cent women and girls) in 430 collective shelters as of 6 July.
  • Basic services in hard-to-reach areas are under enormous strain or are non-functional. Nationwide, 3 hospitals and 35 PHCCs are non-operational, with access to lifesaving services particularly challenging in conflict-affected areas.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Ongoing military activity, despite an overall decline in the intensity and reach of hostilities, continues to pose risks to civilians, hinder safe return, and prolong humanitarian needs among people in Lebanon. Israeli military airstrikes, demolitions, and localized military operations in South and Nabatieh governorates persisted throughout the reporting period. Though the security environment has notably improved since the most recent ceasefire announcement, continued military activity in the south perpetuates further protection risks, prolongs displacement for those seeking to return, and further drives humanitarian needs throughout the country.

Population movements continue to shift rapidly. Between 2 and 6 July**, the number of people residing in collective shelters declined by over 10,000 (21.5 per cent), from 47,143 people in 430 shelters to 37,000 people in 354 shelters**.As of 2 July, the DTM recorded 646,107 returnees, an increase of 123,000 people returning (23 per cent) since 25 June, with most returns occurring in South and Nabatieh governorates. Despite rising return numbers, return movements remain fluid, cautious, and often reversible as families evaluate the extent of damage, safety conditions, and access to essential services. Continued support for basic services, shelter, unexploded ordnance (UXO) clearance, and early recovery remain essential to sustain safe and dignified returns.

Displacement levels have declined over the last two weeks but remain significant, with 499,784 people still displaced. While returns continue, many households remain unable to return safely due to inaccessibility, insecurity, widespread housing damage, and strained or destroyed essential services in areas of origin, resulting in sustained or repeated displacement and increased strain on host communities. Alongside dignified shelter, food security and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs, displaced populations are facing declining economic capacity to maintain current housing arrangements, lack or loss of civil documentation hindering service access, and growing MHPSS needs, heightening protection concerns as displacement becomes increasingly prolonged.

Collective shelter populations have continued to decrease; however, displacement remains concentrated in a few governorates. Beirut continues to host the largest share of displaced in collective shelters, with 14,700 people across 73 shelters, despite a reduction of 3,835 people in collective shelters over the reporting period. South and Nabatieh governorates together host approximately 9,730 people in 70 shelters and remain key areas of displacement. At the same time, new, longer-term collective shelters are being established, particularly in the South and Nabatieh governorates, reflecting the needs of households currently unable to return, or experiencing secondary displacement.

Basic services in hard-to-reach areas are non-functional or under critical strain. According to WHO, three hospitals in the Israeli-declared military area remain non-operational: Bint Jbeil Public Hospital and Salah Ghandour Hospital in Bint Jbeil district (Nabatieh) and Salah Ghandour Hospital in Marjaayoun (Nabatieh). Those seeking services in operational hospitals in these areas face critical access constraints as hospitals continue to encounter challenges in fully reinstating lifesaving services, such as maternity care. Furthermore, the Ministry of Public Health reports that 35 Primary Health Care Facilities (PHCCs) are closed countrywide, 11 within the Israeli-declared military area, creating further barriers to accessing health services and heightening strain on remaining PHCCs. Continued displacement dynamics, fluid shelter populations, access restrictions, and attacks on healthcare are complicating the continuity of services, especially in hard-to-reach areas.

The Ministry of Public Health reported 4,319 people killed (including 392 Women and 253 children) and 12,203 injured (1,450 women and 1,036 children) as of 6 July. 135 health care professionals have been killed on duty and 406 reported as injured since 2 March.

Funding constraints remain a major challenge to sustaining humanitarian assistance. As of 6 July, the 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal has received $269 million, or 42.2 per cent of the $639.9 million requested.

title: PDC Bavi Response CNMI and Guam: Next 96 Hours Situation Update as of 1500 ChST (Guam) 07 July / 0500Z 07 July 2026
content:
Logistics corridor (air and sea access)

STAR Marianas Air has canceled all inter-island flights, while A.B. Won Pat International Airport resumed flight operations on 7 July as Guam moved to Condition of Readiness 4 and cleared its main roads late Tuesday morning. The U.S. Coast Guard reports the seaports of Guam, Saipan, Tinian, and Rota remain closed to commercial traffic under Port Heavy Weather Condition Zulu as crews assess waterways by boat and aircraft. In Apra Harbor, Buoy 2 was found off station in the middle of the channel with several range day boards damaged, prompting a Broadcast Notice to Mariners. Access to Tinian and Rota remains more difficult.
Surface resupply off the commercial port remains on hold.

Emergency power and fuel

Power outages remain widespread across the CNMI and southern Guam, with initial reports indicating significant damage to the electrical grid. Critical facilities in Guam, including Guam Memorial Hospital, Andersen Air Force Base, and Camp Blaz, continue operating on limited power while restoration crews deploy behind the canceled typhoon warning. In the CNMI, the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation expects power and water for essential services to begin returning Tuesday night. Power generation fuel remains sufficient on Saipan and Tinian, but Rota has only 7–8 days of fuel remaining before its next scheduled delivery on 17 July, creating an increasing risk if outages persist.

Hospital and casualty care (health system)

No casualties have been reported across Guam and the CNMI as damage assessments get underway. In Guam, health services are resuming: Guam Memorial Hospital restored visitation by midday Tuesday, Guam Regional Medical City resumes normal outpatient care on 8 July, and U.S. Naval Hospital Guam, which canceled outpatient services on 6–7 July, remains fully postured to provide emergency care. title: Situational Report - Response to Venezuela Earthquakes (July 8th, 2026)
content:
Highlights

• The humanitarian crisis continues to evolve following the twin earthquakes of 24 June. According to OCHA (7 July), 3,685 people have died, 16,740 have been injured, more than 1,000 aftershocks have been recorded and 6,462 people have been rescued, with La Guaira remaining the hardest-hit state. Authorities also report that 17,907 people have been left without housing, increasing humanitarian needs across affected communities.

• The response is progressively shifting from life-saving search and rescue to sustained humanitarian assistance, with temporary camps expanding and growing needs in health, shelter, safe water, sanitation, protection and education.
Humanitarian actors continue scaling up multisectoral support.

• Child protection concerns continue to intensify. Children remain at heightened risk of family separation, violence, psychosocial distress and disrupted education, reinforcing the need for specialised protection and mental health services.

• Assessments continue to confirm a severe humanitarian crisis, including widespread housing destruction, damaged public infrastructure, overwhelmed health services and critical water and sanitation needs. Authorities report 856 affected buildings, including 190 collapsed structures, while preliminary estimates place direct physical damage at USD 37 billion.

• Preliminary estimates indicate USD 37 billion in direct physical damage, underscoring that humanitarian needs will extend beyond emergency relief into recovery, reconstruction and restoration of essential services.

• Plan International with partners has already reached more than 1,635 people across Distrito Capital and Miranda with psychosocial support, primary health care and emergency relief items, while continuing to scale up operations.

title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #2 (9th July 2026)
content:
Two weeks after the 24 June seismic doublet (magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, 39 seconds apart), Venezuela's emergency has shifted from acute search and rescue into sustained, multi-sector humanitarian operations, even as rescuers occasionally still find survivors and already-weakened buildings continue to collapse.

The official death toll stands at 3,535, with 16,740 people injured and nearly 18,000 displaced. Authorities now report more than 940 aftershocks. Buildings damaged are reported between 856 (government) and 2,501 (OCHA/ partner tracking), including 190 confirmed collapses.

More than 55,000 people remain unaccounted for on the national missing-persons platform, of which 123 are children. Authorities report 80 operational transitional camps supporting the displaced population.

Independent satellite-based analysis (ANOVA Policy Research, with Microsoft AI for Good) suggests population exposure in La Guaira's coastal corridor may be up to three times higher than official figures capture, due to outdated census frameworks and under-counted floating population. Of an estimated 403,784 residents across seven La Guaira parishes, roughly 73,500 lived in structures with observable damage, and 37,600 in structures with severe damage or collapse — the group most likely to need transitional or permanent housing.

The UNDRR assessment estimates approximately USD 37 billion in direct damage economy-wide, of which roughly USD 24 billion is concentrated in housing, businesses, schools, hospitals, and public facilities, alongside a separate preliminary UNDP estimate of USD 6.7 billion, equivalent to 6% of GDP.

title: LAO: Flood - 06-2026 - Flooding and landslide caused by Typhoon Maysak #3 (2026-07-08)
content:
Description

Following the widespread flooding reported across several provinces after Typhoon Maysak's passage, heavy and persistent rainfall continued to affect parts of the Lao PDR on 7–8 July 2026. According to the latest forecast from the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH), unstable weather conditions are expected to persist across multiple provinces, with rainfall probabilities ranging from approximately 25 to 65 per cent. Areas with higher rainfall probabilities remain at risk of continued flooding, flash floods and localised landslides.

As of 7–8 July 2026, flooding has significantly affected Kounkham and Nakai districts in Khammouane Province in central Lao PDR. Rising water levels have inundated residential areas, agricultural land and key transportation routes. The Kounkham–Kong Lor road section between Nakham and Nakang villages has been submerged and is impassable to all vehicles. Floodwaters have entered houses in Nakang, Kaeng, and Muang Namsang villages, while agricultural land and rice fields have also been inundated, threatening livelihoods and food production.

Flooding has also isolated several communities. Road access to Nong Hang Kao village has been completely cut off. In Natan village, Nakai District, water levels continued to rise on 8 July, reaching levels close to the second floors of residential houses in several locations. Residents have begun relocating livestock and valuable household belongings to safer areas using motorized boats as floodwaters continue to rise.

In addition to flooding, a landslide occurred on the morning of 8 July along National Road 8A between Phou Pha Man and Khoun Ngeun villages in Kounkham District, temporarily blocking traffic and further disrupting transportation. Authorities continue to monitor the situation closely as rainfall is forecast to continue, increasing the risk of additional flooding and landslides. At the time of reporting, no casualties have been officially reported, while damage assessments remain ongoing.

Local authorities have deployed technical teams to monitor flood levels in high-risk areas and instructed village authorities to maintain 24-hour surveillance. Preparations are underway for the possible evacuation of residents should water levels continue to rise, while district-owned motorised boats and emergency equipment have been positioned to support evacuation and rescue operations if required. Authorities have also issued travel advisories warning the public to avoid flooded roads and the landslide-affected section of National Road 8A. Government agencies remain on high alert as continued rainfall is forecast across the province.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - BDRCS-IFRC-PMO-Monsoon Situation Report 3 #3 (2026-07-08)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

The monsoon depression over south Jharkhand and adjoining Odisha has weakened into a well-marked low-pressure area over East Madhya Pradesh and adjoining regions and is expected to continue weakening as it moves west northwestward. However, a steep pressure gradient persists over the North Bay, while the monsoon trough extends across southern Bangladesh. Consequently, monsoon activity remains active over Bangladesh and strong over the North Bay. Local Cautionary Signal No. 3 remains in force for the seaports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla, and Payra. Fishing boats and trawlers have been advised to remain close to the coast and operate with caution until further notice. Very heavy rainfall (≥88 mm/day) is forecast across Cox's Bazar District from 8 to 12 July, with the highest daily accumulation expected in Teknaf (up to 182 mm). The forecast indicates that very heavy rainfall will persist throughout the five-day period. In particular, Ukhiya, Teknaf, Ramu, Cox's Bazar Sadar, Maheshkhali, and Chakaria are expected to experience consistently very heavy rainfall, increasing the risk of flash flooding, waterlogging, landslides, and localized disruptions।. According to the latest forecast, above-normal rainfall is expected across parts of Sylhet, Mymensingh, and Chattogram divisions, with heavy upstream rainfall potentially contributing to rapid inundation and flash flooding between 5-12 July 2026. The situation is being aggravated by heavy rainfall in the adjoining upstream areas of Meghalaya, Assam, the Barak Basin and Tripura, in India. The analysis made by the Needs Assessment Working Group Bangladesh estimates that approximately 1.95 million people across 12 districts, 70 upazilas, and 585 unions potentially impacted to flood impacts (and probable landslides in some areas), including a significant number of children and older persons.Cox’s Bazar According to the flood risk analysis, Cox’s Bazar is one among the districts at the highest risk of flash flood incidents. An estimate of approximately 504,500 people across 8 upazilas and 74 unions in Cox’s Bazar could potentially be exposed to flashfoods, including 66,065 children under five, 187,476 children and adolescents (5-19 years), and 31,638 older persons. As of 1500 hours (BST) Cox’s Bazar has faced 506 mm of rainfall since 4 July 2026, and 150-380 mm rainfall has been forecasted for next 72 hours. This situation is reflecting potential risk for whole Cox’s Bazar. In the Camp settlement, where soils have already been saturated following heavy rainfalls and recent landslides, additional rainfall is likely to increase the probability of flash flooding, slope failures, and further landslides, particularly in low-lying and steep hill side areas. Humanitarian operations may face temporary access constraints due to inundated roads, damaged pathways and retaining walls, while disruptions to WASH services, shelter conditions, and humanitarian logistics may increase the vulnerability of affected populations.

Risk Analysis

Across the 33 Camps: Between 5 and 8 July 2026, a total of 252 weather-related incidents were reported, affecting 5,195 households (24,614 people) across the 33 camps. The incident caused damage to 2,553 shelters and displaced 4,126 individuals. To date, 18 fatalities and 24 injuries have been recorded. These figures underscore the significant humanitarian impact of the ongoing monsoon conditions and highlight the need for continued monitoring, preparedness, and response efforts, particularly in areas at heightened risk of flooding, water logging, and landslides. In BDRCS Priority Camps (11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19), approximately 93 incidents (36%) with 1,564 Households or 7,417 Individuals (30%) are affected. These incidents have caused significant impacts to infrastructures inside the camp including 1,190 damaged shelters (47%), and 50 damaged WASH facilities (water points, latrines) which is 27% total. Additionally, 7 deaths (70%) have been reported within these camps due to landslide. Impact on BDRCS Priority Camps Remarks: The % reflected above are computed in reference to the total data reported per category (e.g. incident, population, shelter, etc.) across the 33 camps. Heavy rainfall has significantly worsened the flood situation across Cox’s Bazar District, with Chakaria and Matamuhuri among the worst-affected areas. Floodwaters have inundated 18 unions and one municipality, affecting an estimated 5,258 families. Over the past 24 hours, temporary flooding has also been reported in parts of Ukhiya, Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar Sadar, and Ramu, disrupting mobility, communication, and normal daily activities. Across the district, at least Three (3) fatalities have been reported: 2 caused by a landslide in Cox’s Bazar Sadar and another due to a mud wall collapse in Pekua Upazila.

title: UNHCR Libya - Operational Update - 31 May 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

Throughout May, UNHCR faced an escalating campaign of online hate speech and calls for the closure of its offices, amplifying significantly across social media platforms. These online activities generated a notable rise in anti-refugee sentiment. On 14 May, residents of the Al-Siraj area in Tripoli organized a protest in front of the UNHCR office, following an online campaign by the Al-Siraj Social Council calling for the office’s closure citing security concerns due to the presence of refugees in the area. UNHCR’s Chief of Mission engaged directly with activists to hear their concerns, with multiple videos of these exchanges circulating on social media.

The Al-Siraj Social Council issued a warning to property owners in the area demanding the immediate eviction of tenants. A video later emerged showing the eviction of refugees living near the UNHCR office, including the demolition of temporary shelters, raising serious protection concerns regarding the safety of and access to assistance for refugees and asylum seekers in the area.

UNHCR’s Chief of Mission was interviewed by TV channel Libya Alahrar. Discussions largely focused on the humanitarian situation of Sudanese arrivals and broader migration concerns, with some engagement aligning with key messaging around the distinction between forced displacement and migration, as well as pressure on Libyan services and communities.

The Call Centre processed over 39,600 calls, of which around 10,600 were escalated to operators from over 7,700 unique individuals, resulting in 590 referrals for further assistance and assessments. Demand for mental health and psychosocial support services continued to rise, with operators also receiving reports of anti-refugee incidents across western Libya, including forced evictions, assaults, arrests, and extortion, particularly in Tripoli and nearby cities.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #15 (08 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 15
Earthquakes in Venezuela
08 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), authorities report more than 1,100 aftershocks.
  • At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state.
  • Official toll: 3,811 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • A total of 6,462 people have been rescued.
  • Tom Fletcher, the United Nations' humanitarian chief, called on Member States and donors to turn solidarity into tangible support.
  • An additional appeal for US$296 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

Situation overview
Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1, 102 aftershocks.

More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 3,811 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced an additional US$296 million appeal under the Humanitarian Response Plan to assist 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.

title: IDN: Drought - 06-2026 - Anticipatory Action: Severe Drought Risk due to El Niño and Positive IOD - Indonesia 2026 #2 (2026-07-09)
content:
Risk Analysis

According to the latest seasonal outlook issued by the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics (BMKG) on 10 June 2026, Indonesia is expected to face an increased risk of drought as El Niño develops during the second half of 2026 with a moderate to strong intensity, compounded by a forecast transition of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) towards a positive phase. These climate conditions are expected to result in a longer and drier dry season across much of the country, with the peak dry season anticipated between August and September 2026. The prolonged dry conditions are likely to reduce the availability of raw water sources, increase demand for clean water distribution, affect hygiene and sanitation conditions, disrupt agricultural production, and elevate the risk of forest and land fires. Based on BMKG forecasts, lessons learned from PMI's 2023 drought operation, and coordination with PMI provincial branches, the highest-risk areas have been identified in Banten, West Java, Central Java, Special Region of Yogyakarta, East Java, Bali, West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), Lampung, and South Sulawesi. Within these ten priority provinces, PMI has identified 83 priority districts for preparedness and early response planning. The impacts of the drought are already being observed in several parts of the country. As of early July 2026, 55 districts across four provinces (West Java – 27, Central Java – 19, East Java – 8, and the Special Region of Yogyakarta – 1) have officially declared a Drought Emergency Alert Status, reflecting the increasing severity of drought conditions and the need for humanitarian assistance. Furthermore, PMI has already initiated clean water distribution operations in nine districts (five in Central Java, two in West Java, one in East Java, and one in the Special Region of Yogyakarta), demonstrating that humanitarian needs have already materialized in several locations while other priority areas remain in the preparedness phase. In response to the evolving situation, PMI has developed a national operational plan integrating Early Action, Emergency Response, and Recovery, with a primary focus on ensuring continued access to safe water for drought-affected communities. Planned interventions include community awareness campaigns on water conservation, pre-positioning of water tanker trucks and emergency WASH supplies, clean water distribution, emergency water treatment and piped water systems, as well as strengthening community capacity in water resource management and preparedness for future dry seasons. This operational focus has been determined based on the current humanitarian needs and existing national response capacities. Government health services remain functional down to the village level and are expected to continue providing essential healthcare throughout the dry season. At the same time, the Government of Indonesia has implemented a range of drought mitigation measures for the agricultural sector, including the expansion of agricultural insurance schemes, the distribution of drought-resistant rice varieties, and the promotion of climate-adaptive farming practices. PMI's intervention is therefore designed to complement government efforts by addressing the most significant humanitarian gap: ensuring access to safe water, promoting hygiene and water conservation practices, and strengthening community preparedness and resilience. Given the evolving nature of the drought and the likelihood of further geographical expansion during the peak dry season, PMI will continue to closely monitor the situation and scale up its operation based on updated forecasts, humanitarian needs, and government emergency declarations.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by Federation

General

Monitor Situation

Summary

IFRC CCD is monitoring and coordinating closely with PMI NHQ for further update from the field and for further support if required

Actions taken by National Society

General

Other

Public Awareness Raising & Sensitization

Pre-positioning of Stocks

Activation / Mobilization of Volunteers

Summary

Following the updated seasonal forecast issued by BMKG, PMI has activated its preparedness measures to strengthen readiness for the anticipated drought. A national operational plan covering Early Action, Emergency Response, and Recovery has been developed, with a primary focus on ensuring access to safe water for communities at risk. The operational plan identifies 10 Priority I provinces and 83 priority districts for preparedness and response planning. PMI Headquarters has conducted a series of coordination meetings with provincial branches to review the seasonal outlook, assess operational readiness, and consolidate provincial operational plans. Based on these discussions, provincial branches have identified priority districts, available response capacities, and initial operational requirements for the upcoming drought season. PMI has also begun mobilizing its existing response capacity. As of early July 2026, clean water distribution has already commenced in nine districts across Central Java, West Java, East Java, and the Special Region of Yogyakarta, supporting communities affected by water shortages. At the national level, PMI is preparing to mobilize its fleet of approximately 195 water tanker trucks and other operational assets to support the anticipated scale-up of operations as drought conditions intensify. In parallel, PMI is coordinating closely with BMKG, BNPB, local governments, and Movement partners to monitor the evolving situation, refine priority areas, and mobilize additional technical and financial support for the operation.

Actions taken by others

1. Early Warning & Monitoring (BMKG): BMKG (Meteorological, Climatological, and Geophysical Agency) is providing regular seasonal updates and climate outlooks. They are monitoring the El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) indicators to provide localized forecasts for regional governments. 2. Coordination & Emergency Status (BNPB/BPBD): The National Disaster Management Authority (BNPB) is coordinating with regional agencies (BPBD) to declare "Emergency Alert" (Siaga Darurat) status in provinces like Central Java, East Java, and NTB. This allows for the mobilization of emergency funds and resources. 3. Weather Modification (TMC): BNPB, in collaboration with the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) and the Indonesian Air Force, is preparing Weather Modification Technology (TMC/Cloud Seeding) to trigger rainfall over strategic reservoirs and fire-prone areas in Kalimantan and Sumatra. 4. Water Infrastructure Management (Ministry of Public Works/PUPR): The Ministry of Public Works and Housing is monitoring water levels in major dams and reservoirs. They are prioritizing water allocation for domestic consumption over irrigation and mobilizing mobile water treatment units to critical areas. 5. Agricultural Support (Ministry of Agriculture): The government is distributing water pumps to farming communities and promoting the use of drought-resistant seed varieties. They are also activating crop insurance schemes (AUTP) to compensate farmers facing harvest failures. 6. Forest Fire Prevention (KLHK): The Ministry of Environment and Forestry has activated forest fire task forces (Manggala Agni) to monitor hotspots and conduct land wetting in peatland areas to prevent fires during the prolonged dry season.

Planned International Response

DREF: Planned

title: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #10, July 8, 2026
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On May 15, the DRC officially declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
  • As of July 7, 1,708 confirmed EVD cases and 580 confirmed EVD deaths had been reported in the DRC, with 20 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths in Uganda.
  • On July 4, the Uganda Ministry of Health reported a positive case of Marburg, a hemorrhagic fever closely related to EVD.
  • In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Haut-Uele, North Kivu and South Kivu.
  • In Uganda, reported cases remain linked to transmission originating in the DRC.
  • In South Sudan, no EVD cases have been confirmed, but risk of an outbreak remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning.
  • We are supporting 89 facilities of different types in the screening, identification and treatment of EVD.
  • Our supported sites have conducted 121,777 EVD screenings and provided treatment to 422 patients, including 132 confirmed cases.
  • We have so far trained 2,208 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention.

With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO and other donors, International Medical Corps teams are actively responding to the outbreak across the region and collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support risk communication in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols.

Across all operational areas, International Medical Corps continues to closely coordinate with the MoH and relevant partners to support case management, screening-and-referral units, facility-based surveillance, mental health, infection prevention and control, logistics, just-in-time training, continuity of essential health services, and water, sanitation and hygiene services. International Medical Corps also is part of broader efforts to expand contact tracing, helping to strengthen mapping, daily monitoring and follow-up activities to address the risk of undetected transmission across operational areas and beyond.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 20 – 26 June 2026
content:
Ukraine steps up its targeting of Russia through a series of strikes that have targeted Crimea’s fuel, power, and transport infrastructure.

Author: Olha Polishchuk - Eastern Europe, Caucasus, and Central Asia Research Manager1,890 political violence events

[...]

Key trends

  • Russian forces continued applying offensive pressure in the Donetsk region, concentrating attacks around Kostiantynivka and north and west of Pokrovsk, but made no confirmed territorial gains as Ukrainian forces held their defensive positions.
  • Russian forces launched at least 43 long-range missile and drone attacks, including on Kyiv city and the surrounding region, and Zhytomyr and Vinnytsia regions.
  • Russian strikes reportedly killed at least 74 civilians across the Kharkiv, Zaporizhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kherson, Sumy, Donetsk, Poltava, and Odesa regions. Ukrainian strikes reportedly killed at least 24 civilians in the Russian-occupied parts of Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhia regions.

The past week was full of important developments in Crimea. Crimean occupation authorities installed by Russia declared a state of emergency in the peninsula on 26 June. This was a direct result of a series of Ukrainian strikes that targeted the peninsula’s fuel, power, and transport infrastructure, systematically affecting both military logistics and daily life for Crimea’s two million residents. On 21 June, authorities banned the sale of fuel to everyone except state agencies, which left the civilian population and businesses without access to gasoline. Moreover, blackouts became persistent in Sevastopol, the peninsula’s largest city, after Ukrainian drones damaged the city’s main power substation on 24 June.

Ukrainian forces have also systematically targeted the logistics network connecting Crimea to mainland Russia and to Russian-occupied southern Ukraine. They attacked the Kerch seaport oil depot, the Port Kavkaz oil terminal across the Kerch Strait, the Kerch Bridge, and a strategic railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal. As a result of the ongoing drone attacks, residents queuing up to leave Crimea caused heavy traffic at the Kerch crossing at the start of what is normally the peninsula's peak tourist season.

President Volodymyr Zelensky described the operation as “carefully calculated” to “create the conditions that will force Russia to choose peace.” Together with the long-range attacks on refineries deep inside Russia, the aim is to affect Russia itself with the negative consequences of the ongoing conflict. But whether this pressure will translate into what Ukraine seeks is far from certain. The question is whether domestic economic disruption can affect Russian authorities' approach to the war.

What the declaration of a state of emergency in Crimea shows is that Ukraine’s drone and missile attacks keep on improving, both in terms of effectiveness and volume. ACLED records at least 55 Ukrainian strikes in Crimea this week, compared to 22 during the entire May. It also demonstrates that Russia is not able to effectively defend one of its most prized and heavily defended territories — a peninsula that has long been treated as an untouchable symbol of its 2014 annexation. Given the campaign’s success in isolating Crimea, Ukraine is likely to sustain this tactic, and increased efforts to strike the Kerch Bridge itself are a likely next step.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #8 (7 July 2026)
content:
The eighth Situation Report provides an update on the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and summarizes IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts as of 7 July. The second page of the report also includes key funding priorities to sustain and scale up urgent assistance.

Highlights

Official figures report 3,685 fatalities, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 people rescued and 17,907 people without housing following the 24 June earthquakes. A total of 856 buildings have also been reported as affected, including 190 total collapses.

A total of 87 transitory camps have been reported, with installed capacity for 20,227 people and 14,634 people currently accommodated. IOM continues supporting shelter, coordination and management of transitory camps, registration, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, community engagement, information management and inter-agency coordination.

To date, IOM has reached 3,638 unique individuals with 6,253 assistance and distribution activities, mainly in health, CCCM/shelter and protection. Urgent additional support is required to improve conditions in transitory camps, expand access to safe water and sanitation, strengthen registration and referrals, and address protection and public health risks.

IOM activities

IOM continues supporting the coordination and management of key transitory camps in La Guaira, including Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande. Support focused on site management, registration, community engagement, service coordination, basic assistance, connectivity, protection and the distribution of essential items. At Estadio César Nieves, the delivery of non-food items to 500 families was confirmed, including buckets, plastic sheeting and kitchen sets.

At Polideportivo José María Vargas, which hosts approximately 460 families, IOM supported meetings with community leaders, institutional visits, partial systematization of the community census and protection actions with the Ombudsperson’s Office, Civil Registry and SAIME. A total of 192 consultations were also provided during a health outreach session. Cumulative health assistance represents the largest sectoral volume of IOM’s response, with 3,318 registered assistance activities.

IOM continues supporting the registration of displaced families, the mapping of transitory camps and site assessments to inform operational planning. IOM also strengthened protection, community engagement, safe referrals, initial case support and inter-agency coordination, including the placement of information materials in key areas of the camps.

IOM planned response

IOM will continue prioritizing temporary shelter, site coordination and management, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, data and needs assessments. Planned actions include improving shelter conditions through tents, bunk beds, safe covered spaces and site planning; expanding access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene; strengthening medical and psychosocial services; and continuing protection referrals, accountability and risk mitigation for violence against women.

Additional funding would allow IOM to scale up emergency shelter, essential items, WASH, protection, health and mental health services, while strengthening registration, information management, mobility monitoring and coordination in transitory camps and affected communities.

title: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society Situation Report 1: Monsoon-triggered landslides and flooding in Cox's Bazar, Bandarban and Chattogram, Bangladesh (7 July 2026, 16:00 HRS)
content:
Overall Situation:

A monsoon depression persisting over south Jharkhand and adjoining Odisha, India, combined with a strong active monsoon current over the North Bay of Bengal, is bringing heavy to very heavy rainfall to Cox's Bazar, Bandarban and Chattogram districts from 6 to 9 July 2026, with cumulative rainfall forecast at 250–400 mm over this period an increase on the previous day's outlook1 . In the 24 hours to 6:00 AM on 7 July, BMD recorded 283 mm of rainfall in Chattogram, 195 mm in Kutubdia, 129 mm in Cox's Bazar and 128 mm in Bandarban, indicating that the heaviest rainfall band has shifted north into Chattogram while remaining severe across all three districts. Local Cautionary Signal No. 3 remains hoisted for the seaports of Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Mongla and Payra and fishing boats have been advised to remain in shelter.

BMD's updated Special Warning Bulletin for Landslide (No. 05/2026, issued 7 July, 13:00 BST) has widened the high-risk classification. Teknaf, Ukhiya and Cox's Bazar Sadar upazilas in Cox's Bazar; Naikhongchhari, Lama and Bandarban Sadar upazilas in Bandarban; and Wards 7, 8, 9 and 14 of Chattogram City Corporation together with Banshkhali upazila in Chattogram are now all classified as high landslide risk with Bandarban Sadar and Banshkhali/Chattogram City Corporation upgraded from medium to high risk since the previous bulletin. Only Rangamati district remains under watch as a comparatively lower risk area1 . The warning has already translated into loss of life. In the early hours of 6 July, three separate landslides struck Rohingya refugee camps (FDMN) in Ukhiya upazila Jamtoli Camp-15, Kutupalong Camp-7 and Balukhali Camp-11 killing eight people, including five children, when hillsides collapsed onto shelters built on unstable slopes. A ninth person died in a separate landslide in Cox's Bazar municipality. Fire Service and Civil Defence personnel, the Armed Police Battalion (APBN) and Rohingya volunteers carried out overnight search-and-rescue operations3 . With rainfall intensifying and risk levels rising across all three districts, the cumulative toll has continued to climb: as of 7 July, 10 fatalities and 88 injuries have been recorded across 170 weather-related incidents since 5 July, and the potential for further casualties and damage remains high over the coming days as forcasted.
